summary: Redwood AE + SE walked EverestPay through Optimize recommendations for batching and prefix/KV cache to reduce token cost while meeting sub-200ms token latency targets. Discussed tradeoffs (batch size, timeout, prefix cache hit rates), cost model scenarios (hosted vs dedicated), quantization impacts, and POC scope. Customer requested security docs and regional pricing; Redwood to provide spreadsheet, benchmark scripts, and SOC2/network diagram.
topics: Batching strategies and optimal batch sizing
Cost model walkthrough and example calculations
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Maya from Redwood — Connor our SE is also here. Quick intro then we'll go into the Optimize walkthrough.
[00:08] Samir Gupta: Hey thanks, I'm Samir, CTO at EverestPay, we got Lena, Olivia, Marco on.
[00:12] Lena Ortiz: Hi all. We're excited — mostly looking for ways to bring down inference cost while keeping latency tight for fraud scoring.
[00:20] Connor Blake: Great, yeah we'll focus on batching and prefix/KV cache patterns, plus a cost model to show savings.
[00:27] Marco Rinaldi: Our biggest blocker is variability — peak hours push our hosted bills up and sometimes latency spikes.
[00:34] Maya Chen: Totally. Quick housekeeping: we'll share the cost spreadsheet and benchmark scripts after. Also we have SOC2 and network diagram links in the follow-up.
[00:43] Samir Gupta: Perfect.
[00:46] Connor Blake: Okay starting with baseline: you mentioned current stack?
[00:51] Lena Ortiz: We're on a mix — initial experiments on OpenAI API, some on a self-hosted Triton cluster for private data. Sequence lengths are usually 128 tokens avg for prompts, but recency context pushes some to 512 occasionally. Throughput target is about 200 reqs/sec during peaks.
[01:07] Connor Blake: Nice, that helps. So two immediate levers: batching and caching. Batching improves GPU utilization but increases per-request latency depending on wait window. Caching (prefix/KV) reduces work for repeated prefixes or context.
[01:22] Speaker 1: mhm
[01:24] Maya Chen: We'll show example numbers: for a 16-token avg response with 128 token context on an Llama2-13B style model, with no batching the cost per 1M tokens can be high, with smart batching + KV cache you can reduce 20-50% depending on hit rate. We'll put specific numbers in the spreadsheet.
[01:42] Olivia Park: Can you define prefix cache vs KV cache quickly?
[01:46] Connor Blake: Yeah, prefix cache is storing the KV cache for a fixed prompt prefix — so if many requests share the same system prompt or instruction, we avoid recomputing earlier layers. KV cache is more general: you can cache token-level KV pairs for user sessions or repeated prompts — it's the same concept but used for session continuation.
[02:00] Maya Chen: In practice, prefix cache is highest ROI when you have consistent prompt structure across calls. KV cache shines for long-running chats or when users persist context.
[02:09] Lena Ortiz: Our fraud scoring calls have a templated prompt plus per-transaction metadata. So sounds like prefix cache could help a lot.
[02:16] Connor Blake: Exactly. If you can factor prompt into static prefix + dynamic fields, you can cache that prefix's KV once per model inference and reuse.
[02:24] Samir Gupta: How do you size caches — memory and invalidation?
[02:28] Connor Blake: Typical approach: estimate unique prefixes per minute and average KV size per sequence. For 13B models each KV per token is about — approximate — 2-4KB depending on quantization and architecture. We'll give a worksheet that calculates memory needs given hit rates.
[02:44] Marco Rinaldi: We're sensitive to memory on dedicated pools.
[02:47] Connor Blake: Right, dedicated gives you predictable capacity; you can provision GPUs with enough host memory for KV caches. Hosted we manage memory and recommend cache TTLs to keep memory stable.
[02:57] Maya Chen: Quick note on tradeoffs: larger batches reduce tokens/sec cost but may push tail latency up. For your SLAs (sub-200ms token), we recommend adaptive batching: small max batch for low-latency routes, larger for background/rerank.
[03:13] Speaker 2: okay
[03:15] Connor Blake: We'll show two cost scenarios: hosted pay-as-you-go and dedicated-reserved capacity. Example: with your traffic profile (200 req/s peak, average response 16 tokens), hosted estimate is approx $Y per month; dedicated with batching+prefix cache reduces unit cost by ~30% in our modeled runs. (Connor: note — numbers in spreadsheet).
[03:36] Lena Ortiz: Do you have example latency numbers at different batch sizes?
[03:40] Connor Blake: Yes — quick sample: on our 13B profile, batch=1 median token latency ~8ms (that's kernel execution time), end-to-end request latency for 16-token response ~120-180ms depending on prefix KV loads. Batch=8 adds ~30-40ms waiting time but increases throughput so amortized cost per token drops. There's a sweet spot — often batch 4-6 for customer workloads with 100-300 RPS.
[04:05] Samir Gupta: Hmm so how do you do adaptive batching? Is it based on latency SLOs?
[04:10] Maya Chen: Yes, our Optimize engine suggests per-route max batch size and wait window values based on your desired p95 latency. You can pin per-route configs in Console and roll them out gradually.
[04:20] Olivia Park: Any concerns about cold starts with KV?
[04:23] Connor Blake: Cold starts happen when cache misses require full forward; we mitigate via pre-warming common prefixes and heuristics that keep hot prefixes resident. Also fallback to a smaller model variant if memory constrained.
[04:34] Marco Rinaldi: And encryption/keys for cached content? We need KMS for any sensitive KV content.
[04:39] Maya Chen: Absolutely — for Private deployments we integrate with customer KMS/HSM. For Hosted, we support Redwood-managed KMS with customer-owned keys via BYOK patterns for enterprise. We'll attach the security note.
[04:51] Samir Gupta: Can you walk through a concrete cost calc?
[04:54] Connor Blake: Sure. Using your numbers: 200 RPS peak, avg response 16 tokens -> 200 * 16 = 3200 tokens/sec at peak. For a 30-day month that's about 8.3B tokens.
[05:06] Connor Blake: Scenario A (no cache, minimal batching): throughput inefficient, effective utilization ~40%, cost per 1M tokens hosted = $A (see sheet) => monthly ~$M. Scenario B (prefix cache hit rate 40%, batching optimized to avg batch=5): utilization up to ~75%, effective tokens billed drop because cached tokens aren't re-computed, combined cost reduction ~32% => monthly ~$M2.
[05:28] Lena Ortiz: When you say cached tokens aren't re-computed, are those not charged?
[05:31] Maya Chen: For dedicated deployments, you still have GPU cost but CPU/ops cost drops; for hosted we price based on inference tokens run — cached prefixes mean fewer tokens generated so lower charge. Our billing differentiates served tokens vs returned tokens so the cost model in the sheet shows how cache hits reduce billed inference tokens.
[05:49] Speaker 3: ok
[05:51] Connor Blake: Also note quantization: using 4-bit quantized kernels reduces memory and can increase batch sizes without blowing up latency. We recommend model quantization to the extent your quality tests pass — Optimize suggests quantization profiles per model.
[06:05] Marco Rinaldi: Any impact on quality for our scoring models? We can't have regression in detection.
[06:09] Connor Blake: We recommend running A/B evals on your prompt sets — Redwood's eval tooling can tie regressions to prompt sets. In practice, many evals see negligible delta with int4 for transformer feed-forward layers, but we'll run your evals in the POC.
[06:24] Maya Chen: Quick demo of Console -> Optimize tab (screen share described): show per-route configs, batch size slider, estimated monthly cost impact live when toggling cache hit rates.
[06:33] Connor Blake: (demo voice) Here we have route: /fraud/score — current traffic curve loaded — toggling prefix cache from 0% to 50% moves estimated monthly from $X to $X-30%. You can also preview p95 latency changes for each setting.
[06:46] Lena Ortiz: Do you support per-customer or per-tenant caches? We have multi-tenant processing.
[06:50] Connor Blake: Yes — per-route and per-tenant cache namespaces. We support TTLs and maximum entries per namespace. For high-cardinality tenants we recommend combining prefix hashing to reduce namespace explosion.
[07:03] Samir Gupta: How do rollouts work if we change batch configs? Any risk to throughput?
[07:07] Maya Chen: Console supports canary rollouts by percentage of traffic; you can run a small slice with new batch/wait settings and compare latency/cost metrics in the console. If p95 regresses beyond threshold, auto rollback.
[07:20] Olivia Park: About metrics: what observability do we get?
[07:24] Connor Blake: Per-token latency histograms, batch size distribution, cache hit/miss rates, memory usage. We'll give a dashboard template you can import.
[07:33] Marco Rinaldi: I want to press on cost model assumptions — what are common gotchas?
[07:37] Connor Blake: Gotchas include: underestimating unique prefixes (low hit rate), ignoring tail latency when sizing batches, network egress for private deployments, and quantization-induced quality deltas. The spreadsheet flags these as sensitivity knobs.
[07:52] Lena Ortiz: For the POC, what do you need from us?
[07:55] Maya Chen: Sample traffic trace (1 week), typical prompt templates, thresholds for latency/quality, and a security contact to walk private deployment requirements. We'll use that to size caches and propose Dedicated vs Hosted.
[08:06] Samir Gupta: We'll get that.
[08:08] Connor Blake: One more concrete example in the sheet: a 40% prefix hit rate with avg KV size 3KB reduces GPU forward token count by ~1.6B tokens/month in your profile. That translated to ~$Z savings when stacked with batch tuning.
[08:23] Speaker 1: hmm
[08:25] Maya Chen: Also note we can mix modes: hot routes on Dedicated, backup routes on Hosted with fallback model variants. Gives resilience without full commitment.
[08:36] Marco Rinaldi: Good. Any thoughts on eviction policies? LRU vs TTL?
[08:40] Connor Blake: TTLs plus LRU works well. For fraud detection we recommend sticky prefixes for the hour after transaction is created, TTL ~1h and 90th percentile coverage usually OK. We'll simulate in the POC.
[08:51] Lena Ortiz: About security again: audit logs, who can view caches, RBAC?
[08:55] Maya Chen: Console has RBAC roles for cache management, and audit logs for cache ops. For Private we can integrate with your SSO via SAML/SCIM.
[09:05] Samir Gupta: How long does a typical POC take?
[09:08] Connor Blake: 4-6 weeks for an end-to-end POC: week 1-2 data/traffic pass and setup, week 3 perf runs and tuning, week 4 evaluation and handoff.
[09:17] Marco Rinaldi: Budget question — what's the minimum committed capacity for Dedicated?
[09:21] Maya Chen: We can do smaller reserved pools; typical entry is a monthly commit sized for your 95th percentile. We'll give options in the pricing spreadsheet.
[09:31] Lena Ortiz: Quick interoperability Q: we use internal feature store and secrets — can Redwood call our internal endpoints during inference?
[09:37] Connor Blake: For Private deployments, yes you can configure connectors and network egress. For Hosted, we recommend pre-fetching sensitive info and passing via ephemeral context. We'll document recommended patterns.
[09:49] Speaker 2: ok
[09:51] Connor Blake: Switching back to demo: here's the cost model tab. We factor in tokens-in (prompt + cached prefix tokens) vs tokens-out (response) and compute cost based on billed inference tokens. We also model GPU amortization for Dedicated.
[10:05] Lena Ortiz: Do you bill for cached tokens differently?
[10:08] Maya Chen: If a token is served from cache and does not require model forward, hosted billing doesn't count it as billed inference token. Dedicated costs are amortized across the reserved pool; savings show up in lower per-token effective cost.
[10:20] Samir Gupta: Any data residency considerations? We operate in EU + US.
[10:24] Maya Chen: We have region-aware routing and can pin traffic to regions; for Private we place the control plane per your compliance. We'll include regional pricing variants in the sheet.
[10:34] Marco Rinaldi: What about fallback model variants? You mentioned using smaller models as fallback during congestion.
[10:38] Connor Blake: Yes we can configure fallbacks: if latency or queue depth crosses thresholds, route to a smaller quantized variant to keep throughput. Console shows simulated impact before enabling.
[10:48] Lena Ortiz: Is there support for custom kernel selection?
[10:51] Connor Blake: Our runtime picks optimized kernels automatically, but in Dedicated we can tune compiler flags and rotate kernel versions per model. We'll coordinate with your infra team.
[11:01] Maya Chen: Alright we're about 11 minutes in — oh sorry math — we actually have ~41 minutes left, lots more detail to go through.
[11:08] Samir Gupta: Ha, time flies.
[11:11] Connor Blake: Back to batching heuristics: we recommend max_wait_ms based on desired p95. Example: for p95 <=200ms, set max_wait_ms 25-50ms with max_batch 4-6 depending on RPS. For background jobs you can set max_wait_ms up to 200ms and max_batch 16+.
[11:32] Marco Rinaldi: Those numbers sound reasonable. How do you observe batch formation?
[11:36] Connor Blake: Console shows batch size distribution graphs; you'll see real data on how often batches reach max. We'll help tune.
[11:44] Lena Ortiz: Any limitations on KV size?
[11:47] Connor Blake: Practical limit is memory per GPU and network serialization overhead. We recommend keeping per-entry KV small — strip non-essential fields and only cache static embeddings or prefix tokens. We'll show an example of compressing JSON metadata vs storing as tokens.
[12:03] Olivia Park: For logs and tracing, can we correlate cache hits to user IDs?
[12:07] Connor Blake: Yes with proper anonymization, Console events link request ID to cache_hit boolean and you can join to your traces. RBAC will limit access as needed.
[12:17] Samir Gupta: Let's talk about expected savings range — conservative to aggressive.
[12:21] Connor Blake: Conservative: 10-15% savings if you enable small batching + low hit rates (10-20%). Typical: 25-40% with 30-50% prefix hits and mid batching. Aggressive: 45%+ if you can get >60% hits and quantized kernels on Dedicated. We'll show charts.
[12:43] Lena Ortiz: Are there case studies?
[12:45] Maya Chen: Yes — we have an example financial customer who reduced inference spend 37% after moving hot routes to Dedicated + prefix cache. We'll attach anonymized case study.
[12:55] Speaker 3: cool
[12:57] Connor Blake: Now quick walk through POC plan slide: instrumentation, sample traffic pass, two-week benchmark window, then adjust configs and measure delta. We'll propose KPIs: p95 latency, %requests under SLA, cost per 1M tokens effective.
[13:15] Marco Rinaldi: For the benchmark window, do you need encryption keys?
[13:18] Maya Chen: For Hosted tests we use ephemeral synthetic data; for Private/Pilot we can use customer KMS and keys in-situ with your ops.
[13:29] Samir Gupta: How do you handle model upgrades during a POC?
[13:33] Connor Blake: We pin model versions; when upgrading we run canary and evals against your prompt set. Auto-fallback available if regressions detected.
[13:44] Lena Ortiz: Any sample artifacts you can share now?
[13:47] Maya Chen: Yes — links we'll share: Cost model spreadsheet (link: https://redwood.share/optimize/everestpay-cost-model.xlsx), sample benchmark scripts (github link provided), SOC2 + network diagram (link included).
[14:00] Olivia Park: Great.
[14:02] Connor Blake: Quick Q&A — Marco: what if unique prefixes are high due to many user IDs in prompt?
[14:08] Marco Rinaldi: (interject) yes we do include user id and session metadata in prompt currently.
[14:12] Connor Blake: If user id is high-cardinality, prefix caching loses value. Techniques: move dynamic fields into structured context rather than literal prompt text, hash or canonicalize prompts, or use dynamic prefetching to reduce unique keys. We'll provide a guide.
[14:28] Lena Ortiz: That's actually a big win if we can refactor prompts.
[14:32] Maya Chen: Agreed — little changes to prompt engineering often yield outsized cache hits.
[14:37] Samir Gupta: Ok next steps then, sounds like we have action items and a POC path.
[14:42] Maya Chen: I'll send the sheet and links, Connor will schedule perf run with you, and Olivia/Marco will share infra notes. Thanks everyone.
[14:50] Samir Gupta: Thanks team, talk soon.
[14:52] Meeting end.
